sections.h2: Does Louisiana have a quitclaim deed?
sections.html:
Louisiana law has no form called a quitclaim deed. The closest thing is a transfer of whatever rights the seller holds, with no guarantee that those rights exist, which Civil Code article 2502 allows.

That article says a person may transfer the rights he has in a thing without warranting them. The transferor does not owe a refund of the price if the transferee is later evicted, and the transfer cannot be rescinded for lesion. Louisiana is a civil law state, so its deed vocabulary follows the Civil Code, and the Orleans Parish clerk lists a Cash Sale, a Credit Sale and a Warranty Deed as the usual sale documents.

Expect the document you sign to carry a Civil Code title such as an act of sale, rather than the words quitclaim deed. The Orleans clerk, for example, describes a deed as an Act of Sale that may take the form of a Cash Sale, Credit Sale or Warranty Deed.

sections.h2: What does a transfer without warranty do and not do?
sections.html:
It moves the seller's rights as they stand, and the buyer takes the risk that those rights are weaker than hoped. Article 2502 adds two points that matter to anyone using this route.

  • The transfer does not raise a presumption that the buyer acted in bad faith.
  • It counts as a just title for acquisitive prescription, so a buyer who then holds the land can build toward ten years of possession.
  • If the seller later acquires ownership of the thing, that later title does not pass to the buyer.
  • The seller does not guarantee the price will be refunded if a third party wins the property.

A full sale works differently. Under article 2503, the warranty against eviction is implied in every sale, and the parties may enlarge or limit it. Even if they exclude it, the seller must still return the price if the buyer is evicted, unless the buyer clearly knew of the risk, declared the purchase to be at his own risk, or the refund duty was expressly excluded. The seller is always liable for an eviction caused by his own act, and any contrary agreement is void.

Article 2500 describes what eviction means: the buyer's loss, or danger of losing, the whole or part of the thing sold because of a third party's earlier right, including undisclosed encumbrances.

sections.h2: What form must a Louisiana deed take?
sections.html:
A transfer of immovable property must be made by authentic act or by an act under private signature. Article 1839 says so, and a transfer made orally can bind the parties only in narrow circumstances, where the property was delivered and the transferor admits the transfer under oath.

An authentic act under article 1833 is a writing executed before a notary public or other authorized officer and two witnesses. The parties, the witnesses and the notary all sign. If a party cannot sign, the notary has that party make a mark.

RequirementSource
Written transfer of immovable property, authentic act or private signatureC.C. art. 1839
Notary or other officer plus two witnesses for an authentic actC.C. art. 1833
Effect against third persons only from filing in the parishC.C. art. 1839
Person responsible for taxes and notice address named in the deedLa. R.S. 9:2721

The authentic act is the form that needs a notary, which is why closings usually run through one.

sections.h2: Where and how is a Louisiana deed recorded?
sections.html:
It is filed with the clerk of court, acting as recorder, in the parish where the property sits. Until it is filed there, the instrument does not bind third persons.

The Orleans Parish clerk shows how the system runs. The Land Records Division at 1340 Poydras Street takes documents by mail, in person or through eRecording vendors, and a cover sheet tells the office to record the document in the mortgage records, the conveyance records, or both. The clerk's staff cannot say which documents to file.

Every deed filed in Louisiana must also name the person responsible for taxes and give the mailing address for tax notices. That person must pass the details to the assessor, so notices go to the right place.

Parish clerks set their own hours, payment methods and add-on charges, so call the office before sending a check.

sections.h2: How much does recording a Louisiana deed cost?
sections.html:
The base fee under La. R.S. 13:844 is $100 for one to five pages, $200 for six to 25 pages and $300 for 26 to 50 pages, with $5 for each page above 50.

ItemFee under R.S. 13:844
Recording, 1 to 5 pages$100
Recording, 6 to 25 pages$200
Recording, 26 to 50 pages$300
Each name indexed after ten$5
Mortgage certificate, first name$20, then $10 per name
Cancelling a single mortgage$50

The base fee includes indexing up to ten names and one certified copy. A document recorded in both the mortgage and conveyance records is charged separately for each. Paper other than 8.5 by 11 or 8.5 by 14 inches carries an extra $20 a page.

Orleans Parish adds a $5 remote access portal fee and a $30 courthouse building fund fee per recording, and the city charges a $325 documentary transaction tax on sales. Check your own parish clerk for its add-ons.

sections.h2: What does Orleans Parish require when a deed is filed?
sections.html:
The Orleans clerk's Land Records Division rejects or surcharges documents with bad margins, and it does not take personal checks. These practical rules come from its published fee sheet and FAQ.

  • The first page needs a two inch top margin, and every page needs one inch at the bottom and both sides, or a $20 surcharge applies.
  • The first page must carry a caption naming the type of act, and the type cannot be smaller than eight point.
  • By mail, send a business check or money order payable to Clerk of Court.
  • eRecording is offered through CSC, ePN and Simplifile.
  • A cover sheet marks the document for the mortgage records, the conveyance records or both.

A sale recorded there also triggers the city's documentary transaction tax, which is $325 per taxable document and falls on the seller. It is paid at recording or billed, and a bill unpaid after 30 days adds interest and a $500 penalty.

sections.h2: When does a transfer of rights work for a seller, and when does it not?
sections.html:
It can fit a transfer between family members, a clean up of a boundary or interest, or a case where the seller honestly cannot vouch for the title. It fits poorly when the buyer is paying full price and needs title insurance.

  • Heirs who have not finished a succession may only hold uncertain rights.
  • A divorce settlement can move one spouse's interest to the other.
  • A buyer who needs the seller to stand behind the title should ask for a full sale with the implied warranty left in place.

An outstanding mortgage, tax lien or judgment is not erased by moving title. A recorded mortgage stays on the record until a cancellation is filed, and Orleans Parish charges $50 to record the cancellation of a single mortgage.

If you want to sell a house with unclear title, an inherited share or a lien, we can read the record with you and explain what a closing would need.

faqs.q: Is a quitclaim deed valid in Louisiana?
faqs.a: Louisiana has no deed by that name, but article 2502 of the Civil Code lets you transfer the rights you hold without warranting them. The paper in the record is usually an act of sale, donation or transfer of rights. It must still meet the form rules for immovable property.

faqs.q: Does a Louisiana deed need a notary?
faqs.a: A transfer of immovable property can be an authentic act or an act under private signature. An authentic act is signed before a notary or other authorized officer and two witnesses. Most closings use a notary for that reason.

faqs.q: Where do I record a deed in Louisiana?
faqs.a: File it with the clerk of court in the parish where the property is located. The instrument affects third persons only from the time it is filed there. In Orleans Parish, that is the Land Records Division at 1340 Poydras Street.

faqs.q: How much does it cost to record a deed in Louisiana?
faqs.a: The base fee is $100 for one to five pages, $200 for six to 25 pages and $300 for 26 to 50 pages. Orleans Parish adds a $5 portal fee and a $30 building fund fee, and other parishes may add their own charges.

faqs.q: Does the seller still warrant title with a no warranty transfer?
faqs.a: No for the rights themselves. Article 2502 says the transferor does not owe a refund if the buyer is evicted. The seller remains liable for his own acts, since article 2503 voids any agreement that excuses a seller from an eviction he caused.
